items.followUp: State two examples of Newton’s third law of motion and identify the action and reaction in each.

rubric.why: The walking example includes the action of the feet pushing the ground backward and the reaction of the ground pushing the person forward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the walking example with its action–reaction pair.

rubric.why: The gun-firing example includes the bullet moving forward and the gun recoiling backward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the gun-firing example with its action–reaction pair.

modelAnswer: When we walk, our feet push the ground backward and the ground pushes us forward.
When a gun fires, the bullet moves forward and the gun recoils backward.

items.followUp: Define stable equilibrium and give one example.

rubric.why: A small displacement takes a body in unstable equilibrium farther from its original position.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a small displacement makes the body move farther from its original position.

rubric.why: After a small displacement, a body in neutral equilibrium remains in its new position.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that after a small displacement the body remains in its new position.

modelAnswer: A body is in unstable equilibrium if a small displacement makes it move farther from its original position.
A body is in neutral equilibrium if, after a small displacement, it remains in its new position.

items.followUp: Resolve a force of 10 N acting at 30° to the horizontal into horizontal and vertical components.

rubric.why: The force is resolved into two components along directions at right angles to each other.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the force is split into two perpendicular components.

rubric.why: The components are related to the force and its angle by the appropriate trigonometric ratios when the angle is measured from the horizontal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving either correct component relation for an angle measured from the horizontal.

modelAnswer: Choose two perpendicular directions, usually horizontal and vertical, and resolve the force along these directions.
If the force F makes an angle θ with the horizontal, its horizontal component is Fₓ = F cos θ and its vertical component is Fᵧ = F sin θ.
